name: Ireland
tagline: English-speaking, EU, and your IB score becomes a number
summary: Ireland is the only English-speaking country left in the EU, and it treats your IB Diploma more precisely than anywhere else: there is a published table that turns your overall IB score into CAO points, and courses are filled strictly by points. As an EU citizen who has lived in the EEA you normally pay no tuition at all under the Free Fees Initiative - only the student contribution, which fell to 2,500 EUR from 2026/27. The catch is that you apply through one central office, CAO, with a closing date of 1 February, and that Irish student accommodation is expensive and scarce.
whyConsider: Everything is taught in English, so there is no language barrier and no language test to plan for.
The IB-to-CAO conversion is published and public: you can work out before you apply roughly which courses your predicted score reaches.

Free Fees Initiative: EU/EEA/Swiss/UK nationals ordinarily resident in the EEA for three of the previous five years pay no tuition on a first undergraduate degree, only the 2,500 EUR student contribution.
A grade 4 or better in Higher Level Mathematics adds 25 bonus CAO points, which is worth roughly a whole IB point.
One application, one fee, up to ten Level 8 course choices in preference order.
watchOuts: CAO closes at 17:00 on 1 February - months before you sit your exams, and you are applying on predicted performance with no idea of the year's points.
Points requirements are not published in advance. They are set each August by supply and demand, so a course that needed 510 points last year can need 543 this year.
Accommodation in Dublin is expensive and in short supply; purpose-built student housing can run well over 1,000 EUR a month and campus rooms are allocated by lottery in many universities.
The 2,500 EUR student contribution is the figure for 2026/27 after a permanent 500 EUR reduction in Budget 2026. It is set politically each year, so confirm the 2027/28 amount before you commit.
The CAO IB conversion table is republished every year for that year's entry. The table below is the one for 2026 entry; check the 2027 version when it appears (usually in late 2026).

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: 24 points and the award of the full IB Diploma. For a Level 8 honours bachelor's degree the minimum is 24 overall including 3 subjects at grade 5 at Higher Level and 3 subjects at grade 4 at Standard Level (the '3 H5' matriculation route), or 24 overall with the Diploma awarded where only '2 H5' is required. Level 7/6 courses require 24 overall and the award of the Diploma.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: The CAO's agreed table compares IB subject grades to Irish Leaving Certificate grades for meeting subject requirements. Higher Level: IB 7 = H1, 6 = H2, 6 = H3, 5 = H4, 5 = H5, 4 = H6, 3 = H7. Standard Level: IB 7 = O1, 6 = O2, 6 = O3, 5 = O4, 5 = O5, 4 = O6. Where a course asks for O6, a grade 4 at Standard Level is the pass mark. This table is used ONLY for meeting subject requirements, never for calculating points.
ibRecognition.gradeConversion: Points are awarded on your overall IB score from a single sitting. IB 45 = 600; 44 = 600; 43 = 594; 42 = 577; 41 = 565; 40 = 553; 39 = 541; 38 = 520; 37 = 508; 36 = 497; 35 = 481; 34 = 466; 33 = 453; 32 = 442; 31 = 430; 30 = 412; 29 = 400; 28 = 389; 27 = 379; 26 = 368; 25 = 359; 24 = 350. The CAO notes these are sample grades and the steps between them are not even, because they are based on statistical comparison with the Leaving Certificate.
notes: Bonus points: 25 additional CAO points for a grade 4 or better in Higher Level Mathematics, provided mathematics is included in the overall award used for the points calculation.
Single sitting only. All subjects must be examined at the same time and points are calculated from that one sitting.

Minimum English: IB English A grade 3 at HL or 4 at SL; English B grade 4 at HL or 6 at SL (4 at either level if you present the IB through English); Literature and Performance 3 at HL or 4 at SL with documentation that it was the English option.

Mathematics: both Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are acceptable, but the CAO document strongly recommends Analysis and Approaches where a course has a Higher Level maths requirement, and says some institutions may make it mandatory.
Ask your IB coordinator to list 'Central Applications Office' among the institutions permitted to access your results, so CAO can pull your May 2027 results directly on release day.
The IB Career-related Certificate is accepted only for Level 6/7 courses in related areas and is scored to a maximum of 390 points.

deadlines.label: CAO online application opens
deadlines.year: 2026 entry - the 2027 timetable was not yet published when this was researched, expect early November 2026
deadlines.notes: Published as "5 November, 12:00" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. For 2026 entry the facility opened at midday on 5 November 2025. Assume the same pattern for 2027 entry and confirm on cao.ie from autumn 2026.

deadlines.label: Discounted application fee deadline
deadlines.notes: Published as "20 January, 17:00" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. Apply online by this date and you pay the discounted fee of 35 EUR. Applications after this date cost more.

deadlines.label: Normal closing date - this is the one that matters
deadlines.notes: Published as "1 February, 17:00" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. Hard deadline for the standard application. Restricted-entry courses (those with tests, interviews or portfolios, including medicine) must be listed by this date and cannot be added later through Change of Mind.

deadlines.label: HPAT test for undergraduate medicine
deadlines.notes: Published as "13-16 February" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. Undergraduate medicine requires the HPAT aptitude test in addition to your points. You must register separately and sit it in the testing window.

deadlines.label: Late applications
deadlines.notes: Published as "5 March to 1 May, 17:00" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. The window opens on 5 March and closes at 17:00 on 1 May. A late application costs more and cannot include restricted-entry courses.

deadlines.label: Change of Mind opens
deadlines.notes: Published as part of "5 May 12:00 to 1 July 17:00" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. Free. You can completely reorder or replace your course choices, except restricted-entry courses.

deadlines.label: Change of Mind closes
deadlines.notes: Published as part of "5 May 12:00 to 1 July 17:00" with no year; the year here is inferred from the intake this profile covers. Use it - it closes days before your IB results arrive.

deadlines.label: Offer rounds
deadlines.notes: Published only as prose: "From early July (Round A) through to Round 5 at the start of October", so no date is recorded here. For 2026 entry offers ran from 6 July to 1 October. Your IB results are released 5-6 July 2027, so you will normally be considered in the main rounds rather than Round A.

steps: From November 2026, register on cao.ie and start your application; pay by 20 January 2027 to get the discounted fee.
List up to ten Level 8 (honours bachelor's) courses and up to ten Level 7/6 courses, strictly in the order you actually want them - Irish offers follow your preference order exactly.

Include any restricted-entry course (medicine, some art and design, some performance courses) before the 1 February closing date, and register separately for HPAT if you are applying to undergraduate medicine.
Ask your IB coordinator to grant the Central Applications Office access to your results so they arrive automatically in July 2027.
Use the free Change of Mind window in May and June 2027 to reorder your list once you have a clearer sense of your predicted grades.
Results are released 5-6 July 2027; CAO converts your overall score to points and matches you against the cut-off for each course in your order of preference.
Accept your offer online by the reply date in that round, then apply for accommodation immediately.
application.selectionNotes: Almost everything is decided by points. CAO ranks all applicants for each course and the cut-off is simply the points of the last person offered a place, which is why the requirement is only known after the fact. Exceptions: undergraduate medicine combines points with the HPAT test; some art, design, architecture, music and drama courses require a portfolio, audition or interview; and a small number of courses run interviews. Those are the 'restricted' courses you must list by 1 February.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: All of them. Ireland teaches its degree programmes in English; Irish (Gaeilge) is required only for a handful of courses such as primary teaching and Irish-language programmes.
language.englishProof: For IB students the CAO document sets the minimum directly: English A grade 3 at HL or 4 at SL; English B grade 4 at HL or 6 at SL (4 at either level if you are presenting the IB through English); Literature and Performance 3 at HL or 4 at SL with supporting documentation. Individual institutions and courses may set a higher bar, and applicants whose school-leaving examinations are more than two years old must supply additional proof of English.
notes: Primary school teaching requires Irish, which effectively closes that route to an IB student from Denmark.
Because your IB was taught in English, you should not normally need IELTS or TOEFL - but confirm with the individual institution, not with CAO.

tuitionEuEea.value: 0 EUR tuition under the Free Fees Initiative for eligible EU/EEA/Swiss/UK students on a first undergraduate degree, plus a student contribution charge of 2,500 EUR per year. Institutions also charge a small compulsory student levy, typically between 80 and 250 EUR.
tuitionEuEea.year: 2026/27 (the 2,500 EUR figure follows the permanent 500 EUR reduction confirmed in Budget 2026; the HEA page still lists 2,500 EUR for 2025/26)

costs.applicationFee: 35 EUR if you apply online by 20 January (discounted rate for 2026 entry). Applying after that date costs more; the standard and late fees were not confirmed on an official page during this research.
notes: Non-EU undergraduate tuition in Ireland is charged per course and varies widely by university and subject; no official national figure was verified during this research, so check the fees page of each institution.

No official national living-cost figure was verified during this research. Individual universities publish their own estimates - check the cost-of-living page of the university you are applying to, and expect Dublin to be considerably more expensive than Galway, Cork or Limerick.
Eligibility for free fees is assessed by the higher education institution you attend, not by CAO.

funding: Free Fees Initiative: the state pays your tuition if you are an EU/EEA/Swiss/UK national who has been ordinarily resident in an EU/EEA/Swiss state or the UK for at least three of the five years before entry, on a first full-time undergraduate course of at least two years. A Danish student who has lived in Denmark qualifies on the residency test.
Danish SU: as a Danish citizen you can normally take SU abroad for a full degree. Apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen in good time.

SUSI grants cover the student contribution for students who meet Irish means and residency tests. Most students moving from Denmark will not meet the residency condition in their first year, so do not plan around it.
University entrance scholarships exist at most Irish universities but are small in number and usually awarded on results after entry.
As an EU citizen you can work in Ireland without a permit, and student jobs are widely available in Dublin, Cork and Galway.
workRights: As an EU/EEA citizen you have the right to work in Ireland with no permit and no hour limit. Non-EU students on a stamp 2 immigration permission may work 20 hours per week during term and 40 hours in official holiday periods, and must also register for an Irish Residence Permit each year and hold private health insurance. Verify the current non-EU rules with the Irish Immigration Service before relying on them.
residency: Nothing to arrange in advance as an EU citizen: you can enter with your Danish passport or national ID card and stay to study with no visa or residence permit. Once you arrive, get a PPS number (Personal Public Service number) from the Department of Social Protection - you need it for a job, a bank account and most public services - and open an Irish bank account. Non-EU students need a visa or preclearance before travelling and must register with immigration and pay the residence permit fee.
housing: Treat this as the main financial risk of studying in Ireland. Dublin in particular has a long-running shortage of rental housing, and purpose-built student accommodation is priced well above a normal shared room. Apply for university-owned accommodation the same day you accept your offer - most Irish universities allocate first-year rooms quickly and several run a lottery when demand exceeds supply. If you miss campus housing, the realistic options are a shared house through Daft.ie, a room in a private student residence, or 'digs' (a room in a family home, often Monday to Friday only), which is common in Dublin and much cheaper. Cork, Galway, Limerick and Maynooth are all easier and cheaper than Dublin. No official national rent figure was verified for this file.
healthcare: Bring your European Health Insurance Card from Denmark; it covers medically necessary public treatment during your stay. EU students are not required to buy private health insurance. Note that Ireland charges for GP visits unless you qualify for a medical card or GP visit card, so budget for that, and most universities run a low-cost student health service on campus. Non-EU students must hold private health insurance as a condition of their immigration permission.

institutions.name: Trinity College Dublin
institutions.note: Ireland's oldest and most internationally recognised university, on a walled city-centre campus; its high-points courses are among the hardest in the country to reach.

institutions.name: University College Dublin
institutions.note: The largest university in Ireland, on a suburban campus at Belfield, with broad first-year entry routes that let you specialise later.

institutions.name: University of Galway
institutions.note: A river-side campus in a small, very sociable west-coast city, with noticeably cheaper living costs than Dublin.

institutions.name: University College Cork
institutions.note: A green campus in Ireland's second city, strong in food, pharma and life sciences with a big multinational employer base nearby.

institutions.name: University of Limerick
institutions.note: A true campus university with a large amount of on-campus student housing and a co-operative education programme that builds paid placements into most degrees.

institutions.name: Dublin City University
institutions.note: Modern, industry-facing and built around paid work placements; cheaper to live near than the city-centre universities.

institutions.name: Maynooth University
institutions.note: A small campus town half an hour from Dublin, with flexible arts and science degrees that let you keep several subjects going into second year.

institutions.name: RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences
institutions.note: A specialist health-sciences institution with a very international student body; EU applicants to medicine apply through CAO and sit the HPAT.

institutions.name: Technological University Dublin
institutions.note: Ireland's largest technological university, practice-focused, with many Level 7 routes that ladder into Level 8 degrees if your points fall short.

institutions.name: Munster Technological University
institutions.note: A hands-on alternative to the research universities in the south, with lower points requirements and strong local industry links.

institutions.name: Atlantic Technological University
institutions.note: Spread across the north-west coast, with the cheapest student living costs in the country and easier entry points.

institutions.name: South East Technological University
institutions.note: A regional technological university in the south-east; a realistic option if your predicted points do not reach the Dublin universities.

institutions.name: National College of Art and Design
institutions.note: Ireland's national art school; entry is a restricted-entry CAO course combining points with a portfolio submission, so it must be listed by 1 February.

institutions.name: Dundalk Institute of Technology
institutions.note: A small institute between Dublin and Belfast with low points requirements and unusually strong music technology provision.
